title: Adjectives II
description: Build natural adjective–noun combinations and distinguish near-synonyms.
objectives: Replace vague adjectives with precise ones

source.title: Advanced Grammar & Vocabulary — Express Publishing
source.note: Lesson vocabulary, examples and written tasks follow the supplied pages. Definitions are condensed for readability; spacing and obvious scan errors are corrected. Hints, explanations and model answers are study aids, not a publisher answer key.

lessons.title: Adjectives in collocations
lessons.body: The document pairs adjectives with the nouns they naturally describe. Its position key is: * before a noun, ** after a noun, generally with be, and *** before or after a noun. Study the book’s collocations and examples below.

lessons.title: Similar meanings: boring, bad and perfect
lessons.body: The document groups near-synonyms by meaning. The nouns and contexts still matter: mundane often describes a job; impeccable often describes appearance, reputation or taste.

lessons.title: Similar meanings: difficult, untidy, clever and ordinary
lessons.body: Use these meaning groups when classifying adjectives and improving the film review. The examples are the combinations shown in the lesson.

vocabulary.definition: Very obvious and without shame, usually something bad.

vocabulary.example: breathtaking view/scenery / For a child of his age, his knowledge of the subject was breathtaking.

vocabulary.definition: So exciting that it holds your attention.
vocabulary.example: It was a gripping tale of murder and intrigue.

vocabulary.definition: Giving a less severe punishment than expected.
vocabulary.example: The judge was lenient and let him off with a fine.
vocabulary.note: Often describes judges, parents or teachers.

vocabulary.example: He was unprepared for his meteoric rise to fame.

vocabulary.definition: Very high and loud, especially a sound.
vocabulary.example: She let out a piercing scream of terror.

vocabulary.definition: Producing a large amount of creative work.
Broad and general, or affecting many things.
vocabulary.example: 'Women are bad drivers' is a sweeping generalisation that is all too common these days. / He proposed sweeping changes to the country's electoral system.

vocabulary.definition: So sound that it is difficult to challenge.

vocabulary.example: Her apartment was dreary and depressing.
He had a mundane job in a local bank.

vocabulary.definition: Of a very high standard, without faults.
Not damaged or spoiled by faults or wrongdoing.
Exhausting and demanding over a long period.
Requiring great physical effort or energetic opposition.

vocabulary.example: The two bedraggled children trudged into the house.

vocabulary.definition: Good at understanding situations and judging them.
Clever in a deceptive or cunning way.
Experienced and clever at gaining an advantage.
Accepted by most people; not extreme.

exerciseGroups.title: Exercise 3 · Improve the review
exerciseGroups.instruction: Replace each numbered general adjective in the review with a more sophisticated word from Exercise 2. Some replacements are a matter of style; compare your choice with a suggested answer.

questions.modelAnswer: a conventional boy / a run-of-the-mill boy
questions.explanation: Conventional stresses ordinary; run-of-the-mill adds an unremarkable quality. Other defensible choices may work in context.

exerciseGroups.passage: For an entertaining evening, I highly recommend the film version of the first J.K. Rowling book, ‘Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone’. It is the story of an otherwise 1) ordinary boy who possesses magical powers. Orphaned as a baby when his parents were killed by an evil wizard, Harry is brought up by his 2) bad and unpleasant relatives, the Dursleys. Everything changes, however, when an untidy stranger turns up on his doorstep. His name is Hagrid and he happens to be the keeper of keys at Hogwart’s School for magicians. So begins Harry’s education at the school and the 3) difficult task of both learning magic and fighting evil. Under the tutelage of the kindly but 4) clever Professor Dumbledore and with the help of his two faithful friends, Ron and Hermione, Harry achieves his goal. Daniel Radcliffe (as Harry) and his co-stars give 5) perfect performances in this refreshing new film in which there’s never a 6) boring moment.
